passage:
Dear Jahnavi,
You asked why I've gone quiet on the group chat. I had been reading my feed for hours, angry at strangers, and I noticed I'd become sharp with everyone, even you. My views were getting stranger too, and everything felt like an emergency. Then I remembered what you said: outrage is what these platforms reward. So I cut my feed down to a few sources I trust, put my phone in the drawer after nine, and started a long book about rivers of all things. Two weeks in, I sleep better and argue less. I'm shaping my mind with whatever I pay attention to. Come over on Saturday and tell me which of my old takes were nonsense 🙂
Akash

qa.q: What does Akash do with the phone after nine?
qa.a: Akash puts the phone in the drawer after nine.

qa.q: How did Akash feel before changing habits, and what did Akash notice?
qa.a: Akash had felt angry and on edge after hours on the feed, becoming sharp with everyone while views got stranger and everything felt like an emergency.

qa.q: What else could Akash try if the anger creeps back?
qa.a: Keep the short list of trusted sources, keep the offline time and the long reading, and talk it over with Jahnavi.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi see Akash's change?
qa.a: Jahnavi may be glad that the remark about outrage landed. The invitation to point out nonsense suggests Akash is open to honest feedback.

grounding: A feed keeps you angry and hooked; curating sources, scheduling offline time, reading long-form, and remembering outrage is rewarded.

passage:
Soo-ah noticed it on a Sunday in Seoul: she had been scrolling for three hours, and she was furious. About a celebrity scandal. About a stranger's opinion on buses. About things that had nothing to do with her life.

Her friend Rafael had texted twice. She hadn't answered.

That evening she met him at the noodle stall. "You look angry," he said.

"I am. I don't even know at what."

"Your feed?"

She laughed, embarrassed. "My feed."

On the walk home she made a plan. She unfollowed ten accounts that only made her angry. She followed two long-form science writers and her local library. She set a rule: no phone after nine, and a paper book on the pillow instead.

Two weeks later she noticed she was sleeping better, and she'd stopped thinking everyone on the bus was an idiot. Rafael noticed too. "You're back," he said.

qa.q: How many accounts did Soo-ah unfollow?
What was Soo-ah feeling after three hours of scrolling?
qa.a: She felt furious and unsettled, angry without knowing exactly why.

qa.q: Which of Soo-ah's changes do you think helped most, and why?
qa.a: Unfollowing anger-bait accounts and setting a no-phone rule after nine, because they cut the outrage and gave her time to read and sleep.

qa.q: How does Rafael see the change in Soo-ah?
qa.a: Rafael notices she seems like herself again, calmer and more present 😊.

grounding: The passage shows someone noticing her feed keeps her angry and hooked, and curating sources, reading long-form and scheduling offline time.

passage:
In the working women's hostel in Bengaluru, lights-out was at eleven, but Tenzin's phone glowed under the blanket till two. Videos about politics, then angrier videos, then comments on the videos. She woke up tired and snapped at the canteen staff over cold idli.

Her roommate Kalyani caught her at breakfast. "You've been different. Short with everyone."

Tenzin wanted to argue, then didn't. "I think it's the phone. It shows me whatever makes me angriest."

"So choose what it shows you."

That week Tenzin deleted the video app for a month. She joined the hostel reading circle on Wednesdays and started a thick novel from the library. She kept one news site she trusted and read it once a day, at lunch.

By the end of the month, she apologised to the canteen staff, and Kalyani found her asleep before eleven, book open on her chest.

qa.q: Until what time did Tenzin's phone glow under the blanket?
How did Tenzin feel in the mornings after late-night scrolling?
qa.a: She felt tired and irritable, snapping at the canteen staff.

qa.q: What small steps helped Tenzin change her habits?
qa.a: Deleting the video app for a month, joining the reading circle, reading a novel and limiting news to one trusted site once a day.

qa.q: How does Kalyani see Tenzin's behaviour at first?
qa.a: Kalyani notices she has become short with everyone and is concerned enough to say so kindly.

grounding: The passage shows someone whose feed keeps her angry and hooked, affecting her mood, who curates sources, reads long-form and schedules offline time.
